title: Generics
summary: Type parameters for functions and types, constraints with extends, and keyof.

steps.title: Generic functions
body: Generics work as in C#: a type parameter keeps the relationship between input and output.
You rarely write `first<number>(...)`: TypeScript infers `T` from the arguments.
Without generics you would write `items: any[]` and lose the type of the result, or write one function per type.

steps.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for `pair`?
code: function makePair<T, U>(a: T, b: U): [T, U] { return [a, b]; }

steps.title: Constraints and keyof
body: `extends` constrains a type parameter, like C# `where T : ...`:
function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T {
`keyof T` is the union of `T`'s property names, and `T[K]` is the type of property `K`:
function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: T[], key: K): T[K][] {
pluck(users, "email");     // error: '"email"' is not assignable to '"name" | "age"'
Generic **types** work too: `type ApiResult<T> = { ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; error: string }`.

steps.prompt: Does the call compile? (`longest` and `pluck` as defined above, `users: { name: string; age: number }[]`)
steps.explain: `longest("a", ["b"])` fails because both arguments must be the same `T`.

steps.prompt: Generics are erased too. What does this print?
code: function wrap<T>(value: T): { value: T; kind: string } {
steps.explain: There is no `typeof T` at run time: the type parameter is gone. `typeof` looks at the actual value, and arrays are `"object"`. (C# generics keep their types at run time; TypeScript's do not.)

steps.title: A typed cache
prompt: Write a generic `createCache<V>()` returning an object with:
- `getOrAdd(key: string, make: () => V): V`: returns the cached value, or calls `make`, stores and returns its result
Use a `Map<string, V>` inside a closure.
template: Dojo.eq('get("zz") is undefined', true, dojoC.get("zz") === undefined);
Dojo.eq('getOrAdd("b") again is cached', 2, dojoC.getOrAdd("b", () => { dojoMade++; return 99; }));
hints: Each member uses the `store` from the closure.

steps.title: Sort by any key
prompt: Write `sortBy<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K, dir: "asc" | "desc" = "asc"): T[]` that returns a sorted **copy**, comparing `item[key]` values with `<` and `>` (they will be strings or numbers).
starter: function sortBy<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K, dir: "asc" | "desc" = "asc"): T[] {
solution: function sortBy<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K, dir: "asc" | "desc" = "asc"): T[] {
return items.toSorted((a, b) => (a[key] < b[key] ? -sign : a[key] > b[key] ? sign : 0));
template: const dojoU = [{ name: "Bo", age: 9 }, { name: "Ada", age: 36 }, { name: "Cy", age: 100 }];
Dojo.eq("numbers compare as numbers", [9, 36, 100], sortBy(dojoU, "age").map(u => u.age));

steps.title: A type-safe groupBy
prompt: function groupBy<T, K extends PropertyKey>(items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => K): Record<K, T[]>
that puts every item in the group named by `key(item)`, keeping the input order inside each group.
The tests check the **types** too, with `// @ts-expect-error` lines that must fail to compile:
- assigning a group to `string[]` (groups hold the original item type),
- reading `g.shipped` when the keys can only be `"paid" | "open"`.
With `any` anywhere in the signature those lines compile, and the step fails with `TS2578: Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive`.
starter: function groupBy(items: any[], key: (item: any) => any): any {
solution: function groupBy<T, K extends PropertyKey>(items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => K): Record<K, T[]> {
template: const orders = [{ id: 1, status: "paid" as const }, { id: 2, status: "open" as const }, { id: 3, status: "paid" as const }];
// @ts-expect-error: the key function can only use real properties
// @ts-expect-error: a group holds orders, not strings
hints: `K extends PropertyKey` means string, number or symbol: anything that can be an object key.
Start with `const out = {} as Record<K, T[]>;` (an empty object cannot be typed any other way), then `(out[k] ??= []).push(item)`.
steps.explain: Generics carry the caller's types through: `T` is the order type and `K` is inferred as `"paid" | "open"` from the key function. `@ts-expect-error` lines are how you test that a type rejects what it should.
